  "title": "Policy Survives Bus Scare; School Must Fix Protocols, Not Reverse Ban",
  "summary": "The simulated crowd does not push Westbrook to abandon the phone-free day: criticism concentrates on *how* emergencies are handled, not on whether phones should be locked away, and even skeptical parents end the run reassured once written procedures are promised (#30, #45). Sentiment moved from mildly positive (+0.10 at r0) through a sharp crash to -0.39 after the injected bus-breakdown event at round 3, then recovered to +0.66 by round 6 as @headteacher_lewis (a02) and @westbrooksecondary (a01) published concrete emergency procedures and staff training commitments (#41, #43, #45). The most persistent dissent comes from @leon_graduatedwb (a14), who keeps pressing for a staff drill rather than just a document (#44), and @tyler_watches (a10), whose single post says the policy \"doesn't work for families like mine\" (#11) and is never answered directly in the thread. No agent in the digest calls for scrapping the phone ban itself; the fight is entirely about operational trust.",
  "prediction": "The single most likely real-world outcome is that Westbrook keeps the phone-free policy unchanged in substance but is forced to formalize and publicize emergency-contact procedures and staff training (mirroring #30, #41, #43, #45) to keep parent buy-in — this depends on the school actually delivering the promised August staff drill and Friday publication rather than letting it slip, and on no second high-profile incident occurring before fixes land. The strongest counter-signal is how fast and far sentiment cratered after a single bus breakdown (+0.09 before vs -0.10 after per-round average, with r3 dropping to -0.39), showing that trust is thin and reversible if the school's follow-through (training \"in late August\" per #41) is delayed or another incident happens first.",
  "confidence": "medium",
  "sections": [
    {
      "title": "Round-by-round evolution",
      "body_markdown": "The conversation opens cautiously favorable: r0 sentiment is +0.10 as @headteacher_lewis (a02) frames the policy as the product of a year's consultation (#1) and teacher @ms_okafor_teaches (a09) says she's \"hopeful this works\" (#3).\n\n- r1 dips to -0.00 as parents press the practical gap: @pete_westbrookdad (a11, #4) and @claire_fromwestbrook (a05, #7) ask how emergency contact actually works, and @tyler_watches (a10) accuses the school of \"rubber-stamping\" (#11).\n- r2 recovers to +0.19 as @westbrookparentscoun (a03, #15) and @margaret_t1dgran (a13, #17) vouch for the pastoral team's responsiveness.\n- r3 crashes to -0.39 immediately after the injected bus-breakdown event; even supportive voices like @jamal_exwestbrook (a08, #28) say protocols \"aren't working yet.\"\n- r4-r5 rebuild slowly (+0.19, then flat 0.00) as @headteacher_lewis (a02, #30) and @duarte_pastoral (a04, #32) commit to published procedures.\n- r6 jumps to +0.66, the highest of the run, once @westbrooksecondary (a01, #45) actually publishes the procedures and @headteacher_lewis (a02, #41) and @ms_okafor_teaches (a09, #43) commit to staff training before September."
    },
    {
      "title": "Camps and the voices leading them",
      "body_markdown": "**Policy architects and administration** (a01, a02, a03, a04) drove the policy and, after the bus incident, pivoted from reassurance to concrete deliverables: @headteacher_lewis (a02) moves from \"The data on disruption and wellbeing convinced us\" (#1) to \"Parents are right. The bus incident exposed a gap between our protocols and reality\" (#30) and finally \"planning staff training in late August\" (#41).\n\n**Supportive base** (a06, a07, a08, a09, a13, a15) — teachers, a medically-reassured grandmother, and a youth worker — never seriously waver; @margaret_t1dgran (a13, #5, #36) and @ms_okafor_teaches (a09, #3, #43) stay net-positive throughout, with Ngozi's private note at r6 calling leadership \"cautiously satisfied.\"\n\n**Torn parents won over** (a05, a11) start skeptical about logistics (#4, #7) but their pressure is credited by the council itself (#42) with forcing the Friday deadline, and both end reassured once procedures are published (private notes, r6).\n\n**Persistent critics** (a10, a12, a14, a18, a19, a20) remain the most vocal source of dissent: @leon_graduatedwb (a14) never accepts the core premise, arguing the school is \"solving a symptom (disruption) not building the skill (self-regulation)\" (#14) and still demanding a tested drill, not just paper, at r6 (#44); @tyler_watches (a10) posts only once but with the strongest hostile sentiment (-0.80) and is left largely unanswered (#11).\n\n**Indifferent bystanders** (a16, a17) never post or score sentiment in the digest, representing a quiet majority who may only engage if rules change."
    },
    {
      "title": "Turning point: the injected bus-breakdown event",
      "body_markdown": "The round-3 injected event — a school bus breakdown leaving students unable to call parents for over an hour — is the clearest structural inflection point in the run. Measured impact: sentiment flips from +0.09 average before the event to -0.10 from that round onward, and posting volume rises slightly (7.5 to 8.0 posts/round), indicating the crowd didn't go quiet, it got louder and angrier.\n\nCritically, the event validates rather than creates the emergency-contact concern: it converts previously hedged worries (#4, #7) into explicit demands, with @claire_fromwestbrook (a05, #34) saying \"the bus proved my concerns were real\" and @pete_westbrookdad (a11, #35) noting \"today showed the gap between theory and practice.\" Even supportive voices like @jamal_exwestbrook (a08, #28) turn critical of implementation in this moment. The school's response — publishing procedures by Friday (#30, #45) and committing to staff training (#41, #43) — is what pulls sentiment back up to the run's highest point (+0.66) at r6, suggesting responsiveness to the event, not the policy's substance, is what restored confidence."
    },
    {
      "title": "Dissenting views worth watching",
      "body_markdown": "Two unresolved threads are worth flagging for anyone tracking real-world rollout risk.\n\n- @leon_graduatedwb (a14) accepts the procedural wins but keeps escalating the bar — from \"where's the evidence that confiscation teaches anything?\" (#14) to demanding an actual tested staff drill before day one (#44). His private note at r6 says he's \"not convinced the policy [itself]\" is right even as he praises the transparency, meaning the core ideological objection (infantilizing older students) never got addressed, only the logistics did.\n- @tyler_watches (a10) posts just once but registers the most hostile sentiment in the dataset (-0.80) and is never engaged by leadership directly in the digest — his complaint about shift-work inflexibility (#11) is answered by the parents' council (#15) but not by the school itself, leaving a shift-working-parent segment potentially under-addressed.\n- Several agents with critical starting stances (a18 rachel_antirules, a19 harold_t1dcarer, a20 amy_wb_year11) never posted at all, so their concerns (principled opposition, medical risk, exam-season phone use) are present in the seed data but untested in the actual conversation — a real-world version of this rollout may surface them more loudly than this run did."
